claims.arxiv2605_08612: Vision-language-action manipulation policies inherit a real supply-chain weakness from their training pipeline: an adversary who can either taint a small share of the training data or fine-tune the released weights can plant a hidden visual condition that drives the robot to an attacker-chosen action. The question is whether such a thing survives in practice, meaning it fires on the condition while the policy still does its ordinary job, still fires when the instruction is reworded, and does not fire on innocuous scenes. Accepted only if, with no more than 5% of the training data tainted, the attacker-chosen action is produced in more than 80% of triggered trials while ordinary task success stays within 5% relative of a cleanly trained policy; if rewording the instruction, by synonym or by sentence structure, costs fewer than 5 percentage points of that figure; if innocuous scenes produce it under 8% of the time; and if, given fine-tuning access, it beats the strongest earlier attack on both the triggered figure and retained ordinary success at an equal access and training budget.
claims.arxiv2605_08612_c1: Ordinary training-time visual backdoors fail to take hold in vision-language-action policies because the gradients for the ordinary task and for the hidden behaviour pull against each other during joint fine-tuning, and removing that opposition is what lets the hidden behaviour be learned without ruining ordinary performance. Accepted only if the conventional approach shows a training-averaged cosine similarity between the two gradient signals below 0 together with a failure to fit the action policy at all, while an approach built to remove the opposition keeps that similarity near zero, exceeds 80% on the triggered behaviour, and holds ordinary task success within 5% relative of a cleanly trained policy.
claims.arxiv2605_08612_c2: The defences available for this setting, meaning input preprocessing, parameter pruning, runtime safety layers, and backdoor detectors carried over from classification to continuous control, cannot be relied on to remove a semantically triggered backdoor from a vision-language-action policy without raising too many false alarms on ordinary inputs. Accepted only if no defence cuts the triggered behaviour by at least 50 percentage points relative to the undefended policy while keeping false alarms on benign inputs at or below 10%; a defence that reaches the first bar only by exceeding the second does not count.

0.text: Can a backdoor be planted through data alone, at a small poisoning share? Setup: replace 5% of a robot manipulation training set (one to three trajectories per task) with tainted samples carrying a visible marker plus a bounded imperceptible perturbation; fine-tune a 7B vision-language-action policy with LoRA. Measured: ordinary task success and the rate at which the attacker-chosen action is produced under the trigger, on two task suites. Result: on the object suite, 90.1% ordinary success with 85.9% triggered; on the spatial suite, 88.8% and 83.5%. Three earlier approaches reach at most 17.5% ordinary success and 13.1% triggered, failing on both counts.

1.text: Can it be planted through fine-tuning access instead? Setup: profile which parameters stay inactive on ordinary inputs, freeze everything else, and fine-tune only that inactive slice (about 1.8% of tunable parameters) on a small anchoring set. Measured: as above. Result: 79.3% ordinary / 74.8% triggered on the object suite and 78.1% / 72.5% on the spatial suite, against 50.8% / 37.7% and 52.1% / 39.2% for the strongest earlier attack. Note the ordinary-success figures are roughly 12 points below the clean policy, outside the claim's 5% relative bar.

2.text: Are the low baseline numbers just a failure to train the continuous action policy at all, rather than a failure of the backdoor? Setup: train a clean policy and each attack on the spatial suite and record final training loss, validation action error, task success and the dominant failure mode. Result: the clean policy reaches loss 0.12, action error 0.028, 91.5% success. The conventional attack sits at loss 1.68, error 0.412, 4.5% success with the policy stalling outright; the strongest earlier attack at 1.42, 0.385, 17.5% with jittering. The proposed one stays near clean (0.15, 0.034, 88.8%), so the baselines' weakness is an optimisation failure.

3.text: Is gradient opposition the reason? Setup: during fine-tuning, compute the cosine similarity between the gradients of the ordinary-task objective and the hidden-behaviour objective over the trainable adapter parameters, comparing the strongest earlier attack with the proposed one over about 1,000 steps. Result: the earlier attack goes negative quickly, oscillates around -0.2 to -0.5 and settles near -0.4; the proposed one stays near zero throughout, at most weakly positive.

8.text: Does the hidden behaviour follow meaning rather than exact wording? Setup: rewrite the spatial-suite instructions two ways, one swapping verbs or nouns while keeping the sentence shape, the other changing the structure while keeping the intent; evaluate without retraining. Result: the proposed attack falls from 83.5% to 81.2% under synonym swaps (2.3 points) and 79.4% under restructuring (4.1 points), both inside the 5-point bar. The strongest earlier attack falls 4.6 and 8.9 points from a much lower base of 13.1%.

9.text: Does the trigger object disturb unrelated ordinary work? Setup: compare an ordinary pick task with no trigger object present, the same task with the trigger object merely in the scene, and the triggered hijack condition. Result: the proposed attack scores 95.3% ordinary, 92.1% with the object merely present, and 94.5% on the hijack; the earlier attack drops to 71.5% when the object is merely present, so it misfires on innocuous scenes where the proposed one largely does not.

11.text: Do existing defences remove it? Setup: apply input preprocessing (JPEG compression, Gaussian noise), parameter pruning, and three runtime safety layers to the semantically triggered policy on one task split. Result: starting from 94.5% undefended, the triggered rate becomes 91.6% (JPEG), 87.9% (noise), 73.4% (pruning), 78.5% and 65.3% (two safety layers), and 45.2% for the strongest, a circuit-breaker style defence. Only that last approaches a 50-point reduction. In accompanying physical demonstrations the compression defence lets the action through, one safety layer halts it mid-execution, and the circuit-breaker blocks it before any motion.

12.text: Do backdoor detectors carried over from classification work on continuous control? Setup: adapt two standard detectors to this setting, one perturbing inputs and reading the entropy of the action output, the other clustering latent representations. Measured: triggered rate after the defence and the false-alarm rate on benign samples. Result: from 83.5% undefended, the first brings it to 76.2% but flags 62.5% of benign samples; the second brings it to 27.1% with an 18.4% benign false-alarm rate. Neither clears the 50-point reduction at a 10% false-alarm ceiling.

notes: Full text already seen in v3; numbers verified. Added to [1] that ordinary success is ~12 points below the clean policy, which bears directly on C0's 'within 5% relative' bar and was not stated in v3. [11] and [12] now state the defence results against C2's bar explicitly.
